subsection: 1. Supports and barriers for selected groups

notes.h: Key terms: inclusion, discrimination, stereotyping and prejudice
points: Inclusion (inclusiveness): providing opportunities so that everyone can take part meaningfully, with dignity and suitable challenge, whatever their background or ability; for example, a club that adjusts a drill so a player with limited mobility can still score.

Discrimination: treating a person or group unfairly because of a characteristic such as gender, age, disability, race or income; for example, a club that refuses a player a place in trials because of their age.
Stereotyping: a fixed, oversimplified belief that all members of a group share certain characteristics; for example, assuming older adults are too frail for strength training.

Prejudice: a pre-judgement or negative attitude towards a group that is not based on reason or experience; for example, a parent who keeps a daughter out of a contact sport because they believe it is not for girls.

notes.b: Women's participation is shaped by practical, social and cultural barriers, alongside supports targeted at women.
points: Support: women's leagues and programmes that give women their own competitive structures.
Support: female coaches and leaders, who act as role models and understand the needs of women participants.
Support: family-friendly timetabling, so that sessions fit around caring responsibilities.
Support: more coverage of major women's events, which makes female athletes more visible; the developments behind this are in the notes on developments over the past twenty years.
Barrier: fewer role models and less media coverage, so girls see fewer women succeeding in sport.
Barrier: body image and self-consciousness, which can deter women from taking part in front of others.
Barrier: unsuitable kit and inadequate changing facilities.
Barrier: caring responsibilities and time pressures.
Barrier: gender stereotypes about which sports are suitable, which steer girls away from some activities.
Barrier: unequal pay and resources in sport.
Stereotyping: a coach who assumes girls will not want to play in a contact sport and does not invite them to trials.
Media: women's sport receives less coverage than men's, and commentary can focus on appearance or personal life rather than performance.

notes.b: Older adults face health-related barriers and stereotypes about ageing, and are supported mainly by programmes designed for their needs.
points: Support: Go for Life, the national programme for sport and physical activity for older people, run by Age & Opportunity with Sport Ireland support.
Support: walking groups and age-friendly classes that suit older adults' pace and abilities.
Support: GP referral, which sends patients to activity programmes.
Support: the social benefits of group activity, such as meeting others and building friendships.
Barrier: health conditions and fear of injury or falling.
Barrier: lack of confidence, and stereotypes about ageing that suggest activity is not for older people.
Barrier: transport to venues.
Barrier: few programmes suited to older adults.
Stereotyping: the view that older adults cannot benefit from strength training, so classes are not offered to them.
Media: older adults' sport is under-represented in coverage.

notes.b: Disabled people face physical and attitudinal barriers, and are supported by accessible venues, adapted sport and trained inclusion staff.
points: Support: accessible venues and transport.
Support: adapted sports such as wheelchair basketball and para-swimming, which keep the core of a sport while changing how it is played.
Support: Sports Inclusion Disability Officers in Local Sports Partnerships, who help clubs and schools include disabled people.
Support: disability sport organisations such as Paralympics Ireland, which governs Paralympic sport in Ireland.
Barrier: inaccessible facilities and transport.
Barrier: lack of adapted equipment.
Barrier: untrained coaches who do not know how to adapt an activity.
Barrier: cost of participation.
Barrier: negative attitudes from others, including staff and other participants.
Stereotyping: the assumption that a person who uses a wheelchair cannot take part in a team game.
Inclusiveness: a club that runs a session in a venue with step-free access and adapted equipment.
Media: coverage of the Paralympic Games has improved, but disability sport in general remains under-represented.

notes.b: People with intellectual disability face barriers in understanding instructions and in supervision, and are supported by clubs and sessions built around their needs.
points: Support: Special Olympics clubs, provided through Special Olympics Ireland, which provides sport for people with intellectual disability.
Support: simplified instructions, such as short, one-step cues and demonstrations.
Support: buddy systems, in which a partner helps a participant follow the session.
Support: inclusive club sessions where people with and without intellectual disability train together.
Barrier: complex instructions that are hard to follow.
Barrier: lack of trained coaches.
Barrier: limited programmes available to join.
Barrier: transport and supervision needs.
Barrier: low expectations from coaches and families.
Stereotyping: assuming a person with intellectual disability cannot learn a skill, so they are given only basic drills.
Media: sport for people with intellectual disability receives little coverage, so its athletes have few visible role models.

notes.b: Participation by different ethnic groups is shaped by language, culture, religion and racism, and supported by anti-racism work and inclusive rules.
points: Support: anti-racism programmes run through sport by Sport Against Racism Ireland (SARI).
Support: inclusive dress rules that allow religious and cultural clothing.
Support: multicultural teams where players from different backgrounds train and play together.
Support: clubs that welcome newcomers and help them learn the sport and its rules.
Barrier: language difficulties with coaches and team information.
Barrier: cultural or religious factors such as dress codes, prayer times and mixed-gender sessions.
Barrier: racism from players, spectators or officials.
Barrier: lack of role models from the same background in a sport.
Barrier: unfamiliar sports, so people do not know how to join in.
Stereotyping: generalisations about players from a particular country, such as assuming their skills or temperament before seeing them play.
Media: coverage can repeat generalisations about players from particular backgrounds, which reinforces stereotypes.

notes.b: Income, time and local place decide access to sport for these groups, and free or subsidised provision is the main support.
points: Support: free or subsidised programmes that remove or reduce fees.
Support: school sport, which gives young people access to activity regardless of home income.
Support: Local Sports Partnership programmes in disadvantaged areas.
Support: free public spaces such as parks, where activity costs nothing.
Barrier: cost of membership fees, kit and travel.
Barrier: lack of local facilities.
Barrier: time pressures from shift work.
Stereotyping: assuming people from lower-income areas are not interested in sport, so they are offered fewer opportunities.
Media: where coverage sits behind a paid subscription, people on low incomes have less access to it.

notes.b: A comparison names the barriers two groups share, then the barriers that differ in their source.
points: Shared barriers: cost and poor local facilities affect both socio-economic groups and people with physical disability.
Shared barriers: stereotypes and negative attitudes affect women, older adults, people with physical disability and ethnic groups, though each group faces different stereotypes.
Different source: for people with intellectual disability the main barriers are complex instructions and supervision needs, while for older adults they are health conditions and fear of falling.
Different source: for women the main barriers are caring responsibilities, body image and kit, while for ethnic groups they are language, cultural and religious factors, and racism.
Different source: for socio-economic groups the barriers are financial and time-related, such as shift work.

questions.prompt: Compare the barriers to physical activity participation for two of the six groups named in the specification.
questions.model: Women and older adults share some barriers and differ in others. Both groups face negative stereotypes: women are steered away from sports seen as unsuitable for them, and older adults are assumed to be too frail for strength training. Both are under-represented in media coverage, and commentary about women can focus on appearance or personal life rather than performance. The main sources of their barriers differ. For women the barriers are largely social and practical: caring responsibilities and time pressures, body image and self-consciousness, unsuitable kit and inadequate changing facilities, and unequal pay and resources in sport. Women also have fewer role models than they need to see women succeeding in sport. For older adults the barriers are largely about health and confidence: health conditions, fear of injury or falling, and lack of confidence, with transport and few suitable programmes adding to them. The difference matters for supports. Women benefit most from female coaches, women's leagues and family-friendly timetabling, while older adults benefit from walking groups, age-friendly classes, Go for Life and GP referral.

questions.prompt: Define stereotyping and give an example of it in physical activity provision.
questions.model: Stereotyping is a fixed, oversimplified belief that all members of a group share certain characteristics. Example: a gym assumes that older adults are too frail for strength training, so it offers them only gentle stretching classes and never tests what they can lift. The belief is applied to every older member regardless of their individual fitness or wishes.

questions.prompt: Describe a barrier and a support to participation for older adults.
questions.model: Barrier: older adults often have health conditions and fear of injury or falling, which keeps them from joining in, especially when they lack confidence in their own ability. Support: walking groups are a common support, because they are low-impact, suit older adults' pace and let people take part socially. A walking group also gives a regular reason to leave the house and an easy way to meet others, which addresses both the fear of falling and the lack of confidence. Go for Life, the national programme for sport and physical activity for older people, is another support, run by Age & Opportunity with Sport Ireland support.
